w: Funded by a tax on the profits of Portugal's India-bound spice fleets, this Manueline monastery rose in the early 1500s near where Vasco da Gama set sail. His remains -- and those of poet Luis de Camoes, who immortalised the voyage in verse -- were moved into carved tombs here in 1880, near the kings he served.
s: Manueline monastery funded by the spice trade
_facts: construction funded by a tax on profits of the Portuguese India Armadas
built in the early 1500s near the launch point of Vasco da Gama's first journey
example of Portuguese Gothic Manueline architecture
da Gama's remains and poet Luis de Camoes' were moved to carved tombs in the nave in 1880, near kings Manuel I and John III

w: Inaugurated in 1966 as the Salazar Bridge, named for the dictator who ordered it built, this Tagus crossing got a new name overnight after the 1974 Carnation Revolution toppled his regime. A railway deck was finally slotted in underneath in 1999, decades after it had first been planned.
_facts: suspension bridge connecting Lisbon to Almada, inaugurated 1966 as Salazar Bridge
named after dictator Antonio de Oliveira Salazar, who ordered its construction
renamed 25 de Abril Bridge after the 1974 Carnation Revolution

w: This riverside monument marks the stretch of the Tagus where Portuguese ships once cast off for India and the Orient, raised on the Belem waterfront to celebrate the whole Age of Discovery in one sweeping structure -- a single monument standing in for an entire era of exploration.

_facts: monument on the northern bank of the Tagus River estuary in Belem
located along the river where ships departed to explore and trade with India and the Orient
celebrates the Portuguese Age of Discovery, 15th-16th centuries

w: The king's riverside palace stood here until the 1755 earthquake levelled it; the Marquis of Pombal then rebuilt the whole square as the grand entrance to his new Baixa district. Government ministries filled its arcades for a century and a half, and the Supreme Court still sits on the plaza today.
s: Rebuilt after 1755, still Lisbon's grand square

w: People have fortified this hilltop since at least the 8th century BC -- Phoenicians, Carthaginians, Romans and Moors all held it before Portuguese forces took it in the 1147 Siege of Lisbon. It went on to serve as royal palace, barracks and even a national archive before settling into life as a museum.
s: 2,500 years of fortification on one hill
_facts: human occupation of the castle hill dates to at least the 8th century BC
successively held by Phoenicians, Carthaginians, Romans and Moors
conquered by the Portuguese in the 1147 Siege of Lisbon
later served as royal palace, military barracks and home of the Torre do Tombo National Archive; now a national monument and museum

w: Founded in 1884 to house the royal family's art collection, this museum fills the former palace of the Marquis of Pombal with over 40,000 pieces spanning a thousand years -- Bosch, Durer, Holbein and Zurbaran all among them, alongside goldware, textiles and ceramics from Europe, Asia, Africa and the Americas.
s: 40,000 works in the Marquis of Pombal's old palace
_facts: founded 1884 to display collections of the royal family and National Academy of Fine Arts
housed in Palacio Alvor-Pombal, former residence of the 1st Marquis of Pombal
over 40,000 items: painting, sculpture, goldware, furniture, textiles, ceramics, prints
notable works by Bosch, Raphael, Holbein the Elder, Zurbaran, Durer, Sequeira and Tiepolo

w: Built from 1747 as a Rococo summer retreat, this 'Portuguese Versailles' later became a gilded prison: Queen Maria I was quietly kept here once mental illness overtook her in the 1780s. A 1934 fire gutted a third of the interior, but the palace was restored and now welcomes the public it once shut out.
s: The 'Portuguese Versailles' -- and a queen's prison
_facts: 18th-century Rococo palace, conceived as a summer retreat for Peter of Braganza
served as a discreet place of incarceration for Queen Maria I once afflicted by mental illness after 1786
known as the 'Portuguese Versailles'
a 1934 fire gutted a third of the interior; palace restored and now open to the public

w: One of the world's most important private art collections lives here, assembled by Armenian oil magnate Calouste Gulbenkian and ranging from Ancient Egyptian relics to Lalique jewellery, with Rembrandts, Renoirs and Turners along the way. The museum underwent an extensive renovation through the mid-2020s.
s: A magnate's private collection, Egypt to Lalique
_facts: one of the world's most important private art collections
founded by Armenian, Portugal-based oil magnate Calouste Gulbenkian
spans Ancient Egypt to the early 20th century, plus Rene Lalique jewellery and painters like Rembrandt, Monet, Renoir, Degas and Turner

w: Portugal's head of state has called this Belem palace home since it stopped being a royal residence, its facade facing the Tagus across Afonso de Albuquerque Square. The complex of buildings, wings, courtyards and gardens has been added to piecemeal from the 18th century right through to the 21st.
_facts: official residence of the President of Portugal
main facade faces Afonso de Albuquerque Square, toward the Tagus
former residence of the Portuguese royal family
complex built up in stages from the 18th to 21st centuries

w: Named for the explorer who first charted a sea route from Europe to India in 1498, this 160-metre lattice tower on the Tagus's north bank is still the tallest structure in Lisbon, rising over the Parque das Nacoes waterfront.
s: Lisbon's tallest structure, named for the explorer

w: A Benedictine monastery until the 1834 dissolution, this building has hosted Portugal's parliament in one form or another ever since -- through monarchy, dictatorship and revolution. A fire in 1895 gave it the facade you see now, and in 1976 it was where the post-Carnation Revolution constitution was drafted.

monasteries dissolved 1834; building repurposed for the Cortes Gerais, has housed parliament since
major fire in 1895 produced the current facade
after the 1974 Carnation Revolution it housed the Constituent Assembly that drafted the 1976 constitution

w: Begun in 1796 to replace the wooden shack the royal family sheltered in after the 1755 earthquake, this neoclassical palace took over a century to build -- interrupted by Napoleon's invading troops in 1807 and decades of political and financial trouble after. It was never quite finished as planned.

_facts: built on the site of a temporary wooden building housing the royal family after the 1755 earthquake and tsunami
construction began 1796, lasted into the late 19th century

w: Built outside the old city walls in the 17th century, this mannerist monastery ranks among Portugal's architectural landmarks -- and doubles as the royal pantheon of the House of Braganza, the resting place of generations of its monarchs.

contains the royal pantheon of the Braganza monarchs

w: Portugal's largest mosque serves as Lisbon's main hub for Islamic worship and community life in the Campolide district, hosting everything from Friday sermons to festive celebrations and Islamic classes for the capital's Muslim community.

w: Queen Maria I opened this opera house in 1793, replacing the one flattened by the 1755 earthquake. Tucked into the Chiado district, its auditorium has held just 844 seats since the very beginning, a small stage for Lisbon's grandest musical nights.

_facts: opened 30 June 1793 by Queen Maria I
